provenance.generatedBy: claude-opus-5-5 · Field Kit v2 Prompt A batch
provenance.notes: Food family batch, event archetype. Strongest budgets in the family: weddings and corporate events carry the build, office drop-off carries the monthly. Ranges are planning figures, not quotes.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Plated, buffet, family-style, stations and passed hors d'oeuvres, each with a sample menu and a per-person starting price the caterer sets
pageStructurePlus.why: Planners and couples choose the service style first and the menu second. A per-person figure for each style is what lets them shortlist.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Who a tasting is for, when tastings run, how many guests can come, the tasting fee and whether it's credited to the catering contract
pageStructurePlus.why: Wedding couples rarely sign a catering contract without a tasting. A clear tasting step moves them from enquiry to the table.

pageStructurePlus.contains: Boxed lunches, hot trays and breakfast spreads with order cut-off times, minimum headcount, delivery windows and paying on account
pageStructurePlus.why: Office managers reorder every week and hate calling. Drop-off is the steady corporate catering money between wedding weekends.

pageStructurePlus.contains: How the caterer collects guest dietary needs, how special plates are labelled and served, and the caterer's own allergen policy in their words
pageStructurePlus.why: Hosts have to account for every guest's needs, and they ask how a caterer handles dietary cards before they ask the price.

pageStructurePlus.section: Event staffing, rentals and bar service
pageStructurePlus.contains: Servers and captains per event size, china, glassware and linen options, bartending service where licensed, setup and cleanup, and what the venue must provide
pageStructurePlus.why: Quotes from two caterers differ mostly in what's included. Clear inclusions win the comparison before anyone asks.

designDirections.name: Drop-off Desk
designDirections.bestFor: Caterers whose steady money is office lunches, boxed meals and drop-off trays
designDirections.headlineSample: Office lunches and drop-off catering across {City}
designDirections.whyItFits: Driftwood's quiet neutrals and old-style serif look like a clean order sheet, and the cards put the tray menu and order cut-off first.

designDirections.name: Event Table
designDirections.bestFor: Full-service caterers selling weddings, showers and corporate events by service style
designDirections.headlineSample: Wedding and event catering in {City}, from tasting to last plate
designDirections.whyItFits: The family combo, Olive Grove. Cream and olive with a bookish serif feel like a laid table, and the event portfolio reads calm and organised.

designDirections.name: Black Tie
designDirections.bestFor: Caterers doing plated dinners, galas and high-end weddings who sell on reputation
designDirections.headlineSample: Plated dinners and galas, catered in {City}
designDirections.whyItFits: Navy and brass on a dark ground feel like an evening reception, and the editorial serif gives menus the weight of a printed place card.

openers.line: Your catering company's Google listing has great reviews and no website, so a couple comparing wedding caterers can't see a menu or a per-person price before they move on.
openers.hook: Open their Maps listing and confirm there's no Website button. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: Here's what would sit behind that button: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your catering spreads on Instagram are beautiful, but weddings, office lunches and galas are all mixed in one feed. A planner wants to see the event type they're booking.
openers.hook: Scroll their grid and note the event types: weddings, corporate, showers. Name one standout setup.
openers.linkLine: Your catering work, sorted by event type: {demo-link}

openers.line: I couldn't find a single starting price for the catering anywhere. Couples with a budget usually shortlist the caterer who gives them a per-person figure first.
openers.hook: Check the listing, posts and any directory profile for a per-person or package price. If none, the angle holds.
openers.linkLine: Catering menus with per-person starting prices: {demo-link}

openers.line: The catering menu on your site downloads as a PDF that's hard to read on a phone. Most planners are reading menus between meetings, not at a desk.
openers.hook: Only if they have a site. Open the menu on your phone and note what happens. Screenshot it for when they reply.
openers.linkLine: The same catering menus as real text: {demo-link}

openers.line: There's no way to check whether the caterer is free on a date without sending an email and waiting. The wedding date is the first thing every couple asks.
openers.hook: Look for a contact form and whether it asks for an event date. Note what it asks for, if anything.
openers.linkLine: A date check that asks the right question first: {demo-link}

openers.line: Engagement season runs from the holidays into February, and that's when couples shortlist wedding caterers. The ones with a tasting booking page fill their spring calendar first.
openers.hook: Use this from November to February. Check for last year's wedding posts to name a venue or season.
openers.linkLine: Wedding catering and tasting booking, ready for January: {demo-link}

openers.line: Office holiday parties get booked in October. An event catering page with a corporate menu and an enquiry form catches the office managers who are searching now.
openers.hook: Use this in September and October. Look for corporate events in their posts from last December.

openers.line: Saw you're hiring event servers for the catering season. Good staff check whether a caterer looks busy and well run before they apply.
openers.hook: Only if they posted a hiring story or a staffing call. Note the role and the date.
openers.linkLine: A catering site with a join-the-event-team section: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts show catered events at venues all over the region. A page that lists the towns and venues you cater keeps couples from assuming you're too far away.
openers.hook: List the venues or towns tagged in their event posts. Note the farthest one.
openers.linkLine: Your catering area and venues on one page: {demo-link}

openers.line: You're on a few venue preferred-caterer lists, and those lists link straight to a Facebook page. The couple clicking through wants menus and a date check.
openers.hook: Search a local venue's site for a preferred vendors page. Check whether it lists them and where it links.
openers.linkLine: Where a venue's link should land: {demo-link}

openers.line: People keep asking in your comments how to book a tasting. A tasting booking step with the fee and dates would turn those questions into catering contracts.
openers.hook: Look for comments or reviews mentioning a tasting. Note one.
openers.linkLine: A tasting booking page for the catering: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your reviews talk about guests going back for seconds and staff who cleaned up perfectly. That belongs next to the wedding catering packages, not three taps away on Google.
openers.hook: Read their reviews and copy one phrase about a specific event. Quote it back if they reply.
openers.linkLine: Your catering reviews next to your packages: {demo-link}

openers.line: Sounds like most of your catering comes through a couple of planners. If one of them retires or moves, the couples who'd have found you through that planner look you up online.
openers.hook: Look for posts thanking a planner or reviews mentioning one. Name the planner only if they tagged them.
openers.linkLine: Where a couple without a planner would land: {demo-link}

openers.line: Your posts show boxed lunches for local offices. Office managers reorder every week, and a drop-off catering order page saves them calling you every Monday.
openers.hook: Look for corporate lunch, boxed lunch or breakfast tray posts. Note the company only if they tagged it.
openers.linkLine: An office lunch catering order page: {demo-link}

openers.line: That {specific recent job} you catered looked stunning. A setup like that is what the next couple wants to see before they book a tasting.
openers.hook: Pick their newest event post and name it exactly: the event type, the venue if tagged and the service style.
openers.linkLine: That event, front and centre on your catering site: {demo-link}

sequence.dm1:
Hi {Owner} — that {specific recent job} you catered looked beautiful.

I looked for a catering site for {Business Name} where a couple could check a date or see a per-person price, and only found your social pages. I put together a sample with menus by service style, a date check and a tasting booking step, with marked placeholders where your photos would go.

Would you like me to send it over?
sequence.dm2:
{Owner} — following up in case this got buried in event week. Here's the sample catering site for {Business Name}: {demo-link}

It has a date check, sample menus by service style, a tasting booking step and an office lunch order page. If it's not for you, say so and I won't message again.
sequence.call:
"Hi, is this {Owner}? I'm {Your Name}, I build websites for caterers here in {City}. I sent you a message a couple of days ago, did it come through?"

IF NO:
"No problem, I know event weeks are a blur. Short version: I built a sample catering site for {Business Name} with a date check, menus by service style and a tasting booking step, with marked placeholders where your photos would go. Can I email you the link?"

IF YES:
"What did you think?"
 → let them talk, don't fill the silence
"The build runs {Build Range}, then {Care Range} a month for hosting and menu updates. For a catering company like yours I'd normally quote about {Build Price}."
"A single wedding deposit covers most of it. Could I take fifteen minutes on a weekday morning, before your prep starts?"

CLOSE:
"I'll send a one-page scope and a deposit invoice. We start the day it clears, and the date check goes live first."

objections.objection: All our catering comes from planners and venues.
objections.handler: "Keep them. The site is where those couples land after the planner says your name. A date check and menus make the planner look good for recommending you."

objections.objection: Every event is custom, so I can't put prices online.
objections.handler: "You don't have to publish a quote. A per-person starting price by service style filters out the budgets you can't serve, and the tasting does the rest."

objections.objection: We're booked solid through next season.
objections.handler: "Then the site raises the floor. A clear starting price and a tasting fee mean the couples who do enquire are the ones worth your Saturdays."

objections.objection: We're on the wedding directories already.
objections.handler: "Keep them. They send couples to compare you with everyone else. Your own site is where the couple stops comparing and books a tasting."

objections.objection: We tried a website and it never brought in a single event.
objections.handler: "It probably had a contact page and no date field. This one asks for the date and headcount first, so every enquiry tells you whether it's worth a call."
"{Build Range}. For you about {Build Price}, because it's a date check, menus by service style, tasting booking and an office lunch page. One wedding deposit covers most of it."

email.subject: Catering site for {Business Name}

sequence.voicemail: "Hi {Owner}, it's {Your Name}. I build websites for caterers in {City}, and I put together a sample catering site for {Business Name} with a date check and tasting booking. I'll email you the link. {Your Phone}. Thanks."
sequence.takedown:
{Owner} — I'm taking the {Business Name} catering demo down on Friday to free up the space.

Should I keep it up for you? One word is fine either way.
sequence.nurture:
Hi {Owner} — engagement season starts at the holidays, and couples shortlist caterers in January. Office party bookings land around now too. Thought of you.

The sample catering site is still here whenever you want it, and nothing's changed on price. {demo-link} if you want another look.

bullets: Anchor the build to one wedding deposit, not to a month of revenue. Caterers think in events, so price in events.
Price sample menus by service style, not by page. Plated, buffet and stations each need their own menu and starting price.
The tasting booking step is its own line. It is the step between an enquiry and a signed catering contract.
Office drop-off ordering is what justifies a monthly fee. Weddings are seasonal; office lunches are every week.
Sell engagement season pages in November and holiday party pages in August, never in the middle of the season.
Charge per venue for venue-specific pages. Each one ranks for a different couple's search.

lineItems.item: Sample menu page per service style
lineItems.description: Max with dietary marks, per-person starting prices, upgrade options and a printable version for the venue.
Max with set tasting dates, a guest limit, fee payment and the fee credited on the contract automatically.

lineItems.item: Office lunch menu with order cut-offs
lineItems.description: Max with boxed lunch builders, minimum headcounts, delivery windows and a request to pay on account.
Max when the guide covers several service styles, bar packages and rentals with photos and a cover the caterer approves.
Max with a guest dietary card form for hosts and the caterer's own allergen policy written and approved by them.
Max when menus, the date check, the tasting step and the pricing guide are all translated.

whatElseYouSell.name: Styled tasting photo day
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "One morning shooting a full catering spread and plated dishes in good light gives every menu page and the pricing guide real food, not stock."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 2, scheduled on a tasting day when the kitchen is already plating.

whatElseYouSell.name: Google profile upkeep for the catering company
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "New event photos and catering posts on your Google profile every week, with the event type named, so people searching for a caterer see you're busy."

whatElseYouSell.name: Review requests after every catered event
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "Two days after the wedding or office party, the host gets a short note asking for a review while the compliments from guests are still coming in."
whatElseYouSell.when: Day 30. The easiest second sale for a caterer.

whatElseYouSell.name: Engagement season wedding catering campaign
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A January push to newly engaged couples that points straight at the tasting booking page, before other caterers fill their spring."
whatElseYouSell.when: Pitch in November, run from late December to February.

whatElseYouSell.name: Holiday office party catering campaign
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "An October push to office managers for holiday party catering, with the corporate menu and a date check ready to go."
whatElseYouSell.when: Pitch in August, run from late September to November.

whatElseYouSell.name: Venue landing pages for the caterer
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A page for each venue you cater at, with past event photos and the kitchen setup there, so couples searching that venue find your catering."
whatElseYouSell.when: Month 3, one venue at a time, starting with the one they cater most.

whatElseYouSell.name: Preferred-vendor one-sheet for planners and venues
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A one-page catering sheet with service styles, starting prices and your date check link that planners and venues can hand to every couple."

whatElseYouSell.name: Bridal show booth kit
whatElseYouSell.pitchLine: "A banner, a tasting card with a booking code and a sign-up page for the bridal show, so couples who sample your catering book a tasting before they leave."
whatElseYouSell.when: Six weeks before the local bridal show, usually January.

withoutAI.pitchLine: "The barn venue where you cater most weekends has a gallery and no date check. You can introduce me to the owner."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Venues book months ahead like caterers do, with bigger budgets. A caterer they trust walks you in.

withoutAI.route: The wedding planners who refer them
withoutAI.whoPays: The planner, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The planner who sends you wedding catering has a feed and no site. Their couples need a page that lists her trusted vendors, starting with you."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Planners refer for a living. A planner you build for keeps referring the caterer and now refers you.

withoutAI.route: The party rental company that supplies their linens
withoutAI.pitchLine: "Your linen and china supplier rents to every caterer and venue in the area and quotes by email. Introduce me."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Rental companies have catalogues to put online and real budgets. The caterer is a steady account with a warm voice.

withoutAI.route: The bartending service they pair with
withoutAI.whoPays: The bartending company, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The bar service you work beside at weddings needs a packages page and a date check too. They'd trust a recommendation from the caterer."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Bar services work the same events with the same couples. The template carries over almost unchanged.

withoutAI.route: The florists and photographers at the same weddings
withoutAI.whoPays: Each vendor, at your normal rate
withoutAI.pitchLine: "Every florist and photographer you see at your catered weddings has the same no-date-check problem. I work the vendor list you already share."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Wedding vendors refer in circles. A caterer is at the centre of most of them.

withoutAI.route: The farm or butcher that supplies them
withoutAI.pitchLine: "The farm that supplies your catering produce sells to restaurants and the public with no order page. A caterer's introduction carries weight there."
withoutAI.whyItWorks: Local producers sell wholesale and retail and need both online. The caterer is a known, paying customer.

withAI.pitchLine: "Couples ask whether the venue is free on their date and get an answer from the calendar at night, with a tour request and the catering partners listed."
withAI.whyItWorks: Venues lose couples who wait a day for a reply. A tool that books tours pays for itself in one booking.

withAI.route: Client intake assistant for the planner
withAI.pitchLine: "Couples describe their wedding, guest count and budget, and the planner gets a summary and suggested vendors, the caterer included."
withAI.whyItWorks: Planners spend first calls collecting the same details. The caterer client vouches for both of you.

withAI.route: Rental quote builder for the rental company
withAI.pitchLine: "A caterer or couple enters guest count and service style, and the rental company gets a draft linen, china and glassware quote to check."
withAI.whyItWorks: Rental quotes are counting work done by hand. The caterer knows exactly what a typical event order looks like.

withAI.route: Bar package planner for the bartending service
withAI.pitchLine: "Hosts enter guest count and event length and get the bar service's own package options to compare, with a date check."
withAI.whyItWorks: Bar companies answer the same how-much-do-we-need question for every event. A planner turns that into a booking.

withAI.route: Timeline helper for the wedding photographer
withAI.pitchLine: "The photographer's couples get a draft wedding day timeline that fits the catering service times, so dinner and the toasts don't collide."
withAI.whyItWorks: Photographers build timelines by hand for every wedding. The caterer's service times make it accurate.

withAI.route: Wholesale order assistant for the farm
withAI.whoPays: The farm or butcher shop, monthly
withAI.pitchLine: "Caterers and restaurants text their weekly order, and the farm gets a clean pick list by customer before harvest day."
withAI.whyItWorks: Small producers take orders by text and lose some. The caterer client knows how food businesses order.

softwareAI.name: Instant enquiry reply with the pricing guide
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every catering enquiry gets the pricing guide and a tasting link within minutes, even on a Saturday when you're serving a wedding."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: At build or day 14. Needs the pricing guide and the reply wording the caterer approves.

softwareAI.name: Event date availability calendar
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Couples see whether your catering team is free on their date before they enquire, and booked dates close themselves when the deposit lands."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Day 14. Needs their current bookings and how many events they can staff on one day.

softwareAI.name: Catering proposal builder with per-person menus
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Pick the service style, the menu and the headcount, and a branded catering proposal with per-person pricing, staffing and rentals is ready to send."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs their menus, per-person prices, staffing rules and a recent proposal to copy the layout.

softwareAI.name: Menu and date question answers on the site
softwareAI.pitchLine: "'Do you do vegan plates' and 'are you free the second Saturday in June' get answered from your catering menus and calendar at midnight, with a tasting link."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs menus, the availability calendar and their dietary policy in writing. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Deposit and balance reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Each catering contract's deposit, second payment and final balance get a polite reminder on schedule, so nobody has to chase a couple for money."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs their payment schedule terms and a payment account.

softwareAI.name: Tasting appointment scheduler
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Couples pick a tasting slot from the dates you set, pay the fee and choose dishes to try, so the kitchen knows what to prep."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2. Needs tasting dates, the fee and the dishes on offer.

softwareAI.name: Proposal drafter from the enquiry form
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The enquiry says forty guests, buffet, barn wedding in May, and you open a drafted catering proposal from your own menus ready to edit."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, after the proposal builder. Needs a handful of past proposals. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Guest dietary card collector
softwareAI.pitchLine: "The host sends one link, each guest enters their meal choice and dietary needs, and the catering team gets a clean list and place-card labels."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their menu choices per event and the wording of their allergen policy.

softwareAI.name: Office lunch reorder reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Office managers who order catering every week get a Friday reminder with last week's order ready to repeat in one tap."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, once office lunch orders are coming through the site. Needs order history.

softwareAI.name: Event timeline and staffing sheet
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every catered event gets a run sheet: load-in, service times, who's on which station and the venue contact, on every server's phone."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs a past run sheet and their staff list.

softwareAI.name: Catering menu description writer
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Describe a new catering dish in a few words and get an appetite-first menu line for proposals and the site, ready to approve."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3, at the next seasonal menu. Needs the chef's notes. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Review reply drafts for catered events
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Every catering review gets a warm reply drafted in your voice that mentions the event and the venue, ready to approve between prep shifts."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 2, alongside the review requests. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Per-head food cost calculator
softwareAI.pitchLine: "See the food and labour cost per guest for each catering menu before you quote, so a cheap buffet doesn't quietly lose money."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4. Needs recipes with yields, supplier prices and their labour rates.

softwareAI.name: Catering enquiry phone answering
softwareAI.pitchLine: "While you're running an event, calls about catering still get answered, the date, headcount and venue captured, and the pricing guide sent."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 4, once they trust the site answers. Needs menus, calendar and policies. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Final headcount and menu lock reminders
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Hosts get reminders to confirm the final headcount and meal choices before your cut-off, so the catering order is locked before you buy food."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 3. Needs their cut-off rules and the event calendar.

softwareAI.name: Corporate catering accounts with monthly invoicing
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Regular office clients order catering on their company account and get one invoice a month, which is how their finance team wants to pay."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, once they have a few repeat office clients. Needs their account terms and accounting export.

softwareAI.name: Purchase list builder from locked menus
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Locked menus and final headcounts for the week turn into one shopping and supplier order list, grouped by vendor, for the chef to check."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 6. Needs recipes with yields and their supplier list. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Portion forecaster by event type
softwareAI.pitchLine: "It learns how much a wedding buffet really eats versus an office lunch, and suggests catering quantities so less food goes home in boxes."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 8, with several months of event records and leftovers noted. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

softwareAI.name: Event staff availability board
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Servers and bartenders mark which catering shifts they can work, and you fill every event from your phone instead of a group text."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 5, for caterers with a pool of part-time event staff. Needs the staff list.

softwareAI.name: Past event knowledge base for event captains
softwareAI.pitchLine: "Captains ask how the kitchen at a venue works or how a past wedding was laid out, and get answers from your own catering notes."
softwareAI.whenAndWhatItTakes: Month 9, for caterers running several events a weekend. Needs run sheets and venue notes. Comes with the AI maintenance retainer.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every independent caterer builds proposals in a word processor at midnight. A per-person catering proposal builder is a product they'll pay for monthly."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: The first caterer taught you the workflow. Caterers have real margins on events and feel the proposal pain every week.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: State caterers' and hospitality association toolkit
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Offer member caterers a date-check site template and a proposal builder as a membership benefit."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Associations need reasons to renew. One deal reaches caterers who already trust the association.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Every venue in your group has a preferred-caterer list in a PDF. A portal with menus and date checks for each caterer books more couples."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Venue groups sell weddings across many properties. Better caterer pages help them close dates.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your catering accounts need date checks and proposals online. Offer the toolkit as a perk to accounts above a volume threshold."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Distributors fight for loyal accounts. Tools that help caterers win events help the distributor sell more food.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Coworking operators' event and lunch catering ordering
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Members host meetings and launches every week. A catering order page with vetted local caterers makes your spaces easier to book."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Operators sell meeting rooms and events. Easy catering is an amenity they can charge for.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: Bridal show organisers' vendor booking pages
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Couples at the show want to book a catering tasting on the spot. A booking page for every exhibitor makes that happen."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Organisers sell booths on results. Tastings booked at the show are a result they can sell next year.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Families ask the funeral home who can cater the reception. A simple partner catering page with set menus and a date request answers that gently."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Funeral homes field this question every week and want a dignified answer. Caterers already serve these receptions.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your meeting rooms and courtyard host events, but there's no kitchen. A catering partner page with menus and a date check sells the event package."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Small hotels outsource food and want to sell events. A caterer partner page is the missing piece.

routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your students cater real events for practice. A booking page with menus and date checks fills the calendar with paying events."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Schools need real events for training and revenue. The caterer client often trained or hires there.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: White-label catering site template for agencies
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your agency picks up caterers and builds a generic site. License my date-check catering template with menus by service style."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Agencies sell the client; you sell them the part that books tastings, already built.

routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: The denomination's regional office or hall network
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "Your halls host receptions and fundraisers every weekend. A shared booking site with approved caterers for each hall would fill them."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Hall networks rent space and need caterer lists. A caterer who serves their halls opens the door.

routesToBiggerBuyer.route: One caterer per venue circuit in the next metro
routesToBiggerBuyer.whoPays: New catering clients in a new metro
routesToBiggerBuyer.pitchLine: "I build for one caterer per venue circuit in {City}. The venues an hour away have their own caterers and none of them have a date check."
routesToBiggerBuyer.whyItWorks: Caterers compete inside a venue circuit, not across a state. Non-competing circuits let you reuse the template and the proof.

upsellLadder.offer: Catering site plus care plan, one contract
upsellLadder.trigger: They say yes to the demo.
upsellLadder.line: "The catering site and the care plan go on one contract, so a seasonal menu change is an email to me."

upsellLadder.trigger: They check a paper diary or a group chat before they can answer a date question on the phone.
upsellLadder.line: "Let couples see your open catering dates themselves, and close a date the moment the deposit lands."

upsellLadder.offer: Review requests after every catered event
upsellLadder.trigger: They finish an event with a happy host and no new review follows within the week.
upsellLadder.line: "That host was thrilled. Let's ask while the guests are still talking about the catering."

upsellLadder.offer: Catering proposal builder with per-person menus
upsellLadder.trigger: They mention spending evenings writing proposals, or a couple says they chose a faster caterer.
upsellLadder.line: "Pick the style, the menu and the headcount, and the catering proposal writes itself."

upsellLadder.trigger: Menu pages still show marked placeholders or dim event phone shots.
upsellLadder.line: "One morning of plated dishes in good light fills every catering menu page and the pricing guide."
